raw_case_text:
In June 2018, a 39-year-old male, one day after the diagnosis of HIV infection, was admitted to our hospital for dizziness and vomiting, which had been ongoing for two weeks prior to his admission. On physical examination, his T was 37.5 C, BP 119/92 mmHg, P 112 bpm, and R 20 breaths/min. Additionally, he had a stiff neck, positive meningeal irritation sign. He had a CD4 cell count and plasma HIV load of 7 cells/muL and 131,000 copies/mL, respectively. CSF analysis revealed a pressure of >400 mmH2O, WBC count of 3 cells/muL, glucose of 2.3 mmol/L, chlorine of 121 mmol/L, and protein of 0.426 g/L, CSF: serum glucose ratio was 0.41. CSF India ink staining revealed Cryptococcus, and CSF culture showed Cryptococcus neoformans. Based on these findings, he was diagnosed with CM. The dizziness and vomiting disappeared after a VP shunt was placed. Antifungal treatment was administered similarly to Case 1 (for 2 weeks; amphotericin B [0.7 mg/kg/day] and 5-flucytosine [100 mg/kg/day], followed by consolidation with fluconazole [400 mg/day]) for 8 weeks. CSF cultures were negative after 10 days. HAART (Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir) was initiated on day 28 of the admission, and he was discharged from the hospital. The patient had visited the hospital regularly for follow-ups. By March 2019, the patient did not feel uncomfortable, ICP was 115-200 mmH2O, CSF protein was 1.06-2.53 g/L, CSF WBC was 5-10 cells/muL, CSF glucose was 2.0-2.8 mmol/L, CSF: serum glucose ratio was 0.46-0.58, CD4 count increased to 82 cells/muL, and the HIV viral load was 0 copies/mL.
However, in April 2019, the patient developed headache and dizziness. One month later, he developed sluggishness. The patient felt that he could endure the headache and did not come to the hospital until June 2019. He was re-admitted with an undetectable viral load and CD4 cell count of 132 cells/muL. On physical examination, he had a T of 38.2 C, P of 92 bpm, BP of 112/74 mmHg, and R of 18 breaths/min. He was conscious and responded slowly. The ICP was 150 mmH2O, CSF protein was 4.67 g/L, CSF WBC was 68 cells/muL, CSF glucose was 1.8 mmol/L, and CSF: serum glucose ratio was 0.38. Etiological investigations revealed an unremarkable CSF analysis. He exhibited a slight decrease in cognitive ability (MoCA score, 26; IHDS score, 8). Brain MRI revealed multiple regions of thickening and meningeal enhancement (Figure 2A). Based on these findings, he was diagnosed with IRIS. The patient responded well to lenalidomide (regimen as in Case 1; one cycle: 25 mg/day for 21 days and no lenalidomide for 7 days according to the manufacturer's instructions), and after one cycle of treatment, he was able to communicate normally. CSF examination revealed the CSF WBC count of 2 cells/muL, CSF glucose of 2.2 mmol/L, CSF: serum glucose ratio was 0.49, CSF protein of 4.08 g/L, and negative CSF cultures. He had a MoCA score of 30 and an IHDS score of 10 after two cycle of treatment. The follow-up plan of the patient was the same as that of Case 1. There was no discomfort during the follow-up after 6 cycles of treatment. The ICP was 150 mmH2O, CSF protein was 1.24 g/L, CSF WBC was 2.0 cells/muL, CSF glucose was 2.5 mmol/L, CSF: serum glucose ratio was 0.53, CD4 count was 111 cells/muL, and HIV viral load was undetectable at 6 cycles of treatment. The patient stopped the treatment in April 2020 after 10 cycles at his discretion. One month later, his CSF analysis results were suggestive of inflammation (CSF WBC count of 5 cells/muL, CSF glucose of 2.1 mmol/L, CSF: serum glucose ratio was 0.41, CSF protein of 1.16 g/L, and negative CSF cultures). However, his cognitive status remained normal (MoCA and IHDS scores increased to 29 and 12, respectively.)
In July 2020, three months after the termination of lenalidomide treatment, the patient developed involuntary right limb tremors and expressive aphasia. On physical examination, he was conscious, mute, and negative for meningeal irritation sign. The patient's MoCA and IHDS scores were both zero. His CSF analysis results were suggestive of inflammation (CSF pressure of 140 mmH2O, CSF WBC of 20 cells/muL, CSF glucose of 2.6 mmol/L, CSF protein of 5.19 g/L, and CSF: serum glucose ratio was 0.45); however, India ink staining yielded negative results, and the etiological investigation was negative. Consequently, paradoxical IRIS was diagnosed. Lenalidomide (25 mg/day) was re-introduced with levetiracetam (500 mg BID). The patient responded rapidly to treatment; 1 cycle following lenalidomide re-introduction, he was communicating well and doing his routine activities unaided (CSF pressure of 175 mm H2O, CSF WBC of 30/muL, CSF glucose of 2.5 mmol/L, CSF protein of 2.0 g/L, CSF: serum glucose ratio was 0.53, MoCA score of 27, and IHDS score of 12). Brain MRI revealed a significantly reduced degree of meningeal enhancement (Figure 2B). After 6 cycles of repeat lenalidomide treatment, his CSF analysis results were normal (CSF pressure of 120 mmH2O, CSF WBC of 10 cells/muL, CSF glucose of 2.4 mmol/L, CSF protein of 0.9 g/L, CSF: serum glucose was 0.51, and negative India ink staining); therefore, lenalidomide treatment was discontinued. At the time of this report, the patient has been followed up for 27 months and has returned to work.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 39-year-old HIV-positive male with previously treated cryptococcal meningitis and a ventriculoperitoneal shunt presented 10 months later with headache, dizziness, fever, and cognitive sluggishness, and subsequently relapsed with right limb tremors and expressive aphasia 3 months after stopping lenalidomide.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In June 2018, 1 day after HIV diagnosis (CD4 7 cells/uL, HIV VL 131,000 copies/mL), the patient was admitted with 2 weeks of dizziness and vomiting and diagnosed with Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis (ICP >400 mmH2O, positive CSF India ink and culture), treated with VP shunting, 2 weeks of amphotericin B plus 5-flucytosine (CSF sterile at day 10), fluconazole consolidation (400 mg/day), and initiation of HAART (tenofovir/lamivudine/dolutegravir) on day 28. Ten months later (April-June 2019, with undetectable HIV VL and CD4 132 cells/uL), he developed headache, dizziness, fever, and sluggishness; after responding to 10 cycles of lenalidomide and self-discontinuing therapy in April 2020, he relapsed in July 2020 with involuntary right limb tremors and complete mutism/expressive aphasia.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV/AIDS and Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis diagnosed in June 2018 status post ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for headache, dizziness, fever, cognitive slowing, and subsequent involuntary right limb tremors and expressive aphasia/mutism. Home medications: tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, dolutegravir, and fluconazole.

objective.physical_examination: Initial June 2018 admission: temperature 37.5 C, BP 119/92 mmHg, pulse 112 beats/min, RR 20 breaths/min, neck stiffness, and positive meningeal signs. June 2019 IRIS admission: temperature 38.2 C, pulse 92 beats/min, BP 112/74 mmHg, slow responses, MoCA 26, IHDS 8. July 2020 relapse (3 months after stopping lenalidomide): conscious, mute (expressive aphasia), involuntary right limb tremors, negative meningeal signs, and MoCA and IHDS scores both 0.
objective.routine_investigations: Plasma HIV viral load remained undetectable (0 copies/mL) during both the June 2019 and July 2020 admissions.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ count rose from 7 cells/uL (June 2018) to 132 cells/uL (June 2019) and 111 cells/uL (cycle 6). June 2019 brain MRI showed multiple regions of meningeal thickening and enhancement, and LP showed ICP 150 mmH2O, WBC 68 cells/uL, markedly elevated protein 4.67 g/L, glucose 1.8 mmol/L (CSF:serum ratio 0.38), and negative CSF cultures. At the July 2020 relapse, LP showed ICP 140 mmH2O, WBC 20 cells/uL, elevated protein 5.19 g/L, glucose 2.6 mmol/L (ratio 0.45), and negative India ink and microbiological workup.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of HIV-associated paradoxical cryptococcal meningitis immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (CM-IRIS) with relapse following premature discontinuation of lenalidomide, confirmed by sterile CSF cultures, undetectable plasma HIV viral load, marked CSF hyperproteinorrachia (4.67-5.19 g/L) and pleocytosis, and meningeal enhancement on brain MRI. Initial 10 cycles of oral lenalidomide (25 mg/day for 21 of 28 days) normalized cognition (MoCA 30, IHDS 10-12) and reduced CSF protein to 1.16-1.24 g/L; following clinical relapse (mutism and right limb tremors, MoCA 0) 3 months after self-discontinuation, re-initiation of lenalidomide (25 mg/day for 6 additional cycles) plus levetiracetam (500 mg twice daily) rapidly restored speech and functional independence within 1 cycle (MoCA 27, IHDS 12), normalized CSF parameters (protein 0.9 g/L) and MRI enhancement by cycle 6, and allowed return to work over 27 months of follow-up.
